I say: The purpose of mentioning it is not what you think, distinguishing the one who was sent upon a straight path from others who are not of his description. Rather, the purpose is to describe him and to describe what he brought of the Sharia, so he combined the two descriptions in one arrangement, as if he said: "You are surely among the messengers, steadfast upon a steadfast path." Also, the indefiniteness (tankīr) in it indicates that he was sent from among the straight paths upon a straight path whose description cannot be grasped.

[Maḥmūd said: "If you say, what is the secret of His saying 'upon a straight path,' since it is known from his being among the messengers that he is so? He answered that the purpose is to describe him and to describe what he brought, so he brought the two descriptions in one arrangement, as if he said: 'You are surely among the messengers upon a steady path.'

Qawman mā undhira ābāʾuhum: a people whose fathers were not warned, as a qualifying description (ṣifa).

[Maḥmūd said: It is a qualifying description, like His saying: "That you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you" (li-tundhira qawman mā atāhum min nadhīr). He said: "The indefinite 'qawman' is described by the clause that follows." And he explained "mā undhira ābāʾuhum" as affirming the warning, taking "mā" as either a verbal noun (maṣdariyya) or a relative (mawṣūla). He said: "The difference in the position of the fāʾ between the two interpretations is that on the first it is connected to the negation as a response to it, meaning that the negation of their being warned is the cause of their heedlessness; and on the second, it is connected to His saying 'innaka la-mina al-mursalīn' (you are surely among the messengers) to warn, as you say: 'We sent you to so-and-so to warn him, for he is heedless,' or 'so he is heedless.'" End of his words. Aḥmad said: He means that on the second interpretation it implies that their heedlessness is the cause of their being warned.]

Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: "That you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you, and We sent no warner to them before you." He explained "mā undhira ābāʾuhum" as affirming the warning.

The explanation of this is that you take "mā" as a verbal noun, meaning "that you may warn a people with the warning of their fathers"; or as a relative and in the accusative as the second object of "tundhira," meaning "a people warned by their fathers about the punishment," like His saying: "We have warned you of a near punishment."

If you say: What is the difference between the connection of "fa-hum ghāfilūn" (so they are heedless) under the two interpretations? I say: On the first, it is connected to the negation, meaning: they were not warned, so they are heedless, since their not being warned is the cause of their heedlessness. On the second, it is connected to "innaka la-mina al-mursalīn" (you are surely among the messengers) to warn, as you say: "We sent you to so-and-so to warn him, for he is heedless," or "so he is heedless."

If you say: How can they be warned while also not warned, given the contradiction with the other verses? I say: There is no contradiction, because the verses negate their being warned, not the warning of their fathers; and their fathers, the earlier ones, were from the descendants of Ismāʿīl, among whom warning existed.

[Maḥmūd said: If you say, how can they be warners under this interpretation while not warned in His saying: "a warner did not come to them before you"? He answered that the verse negates their being warned, not the warning of their fathers; and their fathers, the earlier ones, were from the descendants of Ismāʿīl, and warning existed among them.

He said: "So what will you do with one of the two interpretations, whose implication is that their fathers were not warned, which is the first interpretation in this verse, along with the second interpretation, whose implication is that they were warned? He answered that their remote fathers were the warned, not their nearer fathers." He said: "Then he illustrated their firm insistence upon disbelief, and that they do not restrain themselves nor return, by making them like those with necks in shackles, held up in that they do not look toward the truth nor lower their heads to it, and like those who are between two barriers, not seeing what is before them nor what is behind them. He said the pronoun refers to the shackles, because the collar of the yoke is at the meeting of its two ends under the chin, with a ring in which is the head of the pole, so one cannot lower his head, and so he remains raised." End of his words. Aḥmad said: If you separate this simile, their firm insistence upon disbelief is likened to the shackles, and their arrogance in refusing the truth and in submitting and humbling themselves to hearing it is likened to being held up, since one held up does not lower his head.

His saying "fa-hiya ilā al-adhqān" (so they are up to the chins) completes the implication of their being held up. The absence of reflection about the earlier generations is likened to a barrier behind them, and the absence of consideration of the coming consequences is likened to a barrier before them.]

Al-qawl (the word): His saying, exalted is He: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humankind, all together." It means: this word has come upon them, has taken hold of them, and has become binding, because they are among those known to die upon disbelief.

Then he illustrates their obstinacy in disbelief, and that there is no way for them to be brought back, by making them like those whose necks are shackled and whose heads are raised (*muqmahin*):

In that they do not turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks toward it, nor lower their heads before it. And [they are] like those enclosed between two barriers, unable to see what is before them or behind them: in that they have no reflection and no perception, and that they are blind to contemplating the signs of God. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿and they are up to the chins﴾? I say: its meaning is: the shackles reach up to the chins and are fastened to them. This is because the collar of the shackle around the neck of the one shackled has its two ends meeting beneath the chin, a ring in which is the head of the rod (*al-'amud*), rising (*nadiran*, i.e. unusually) from the ring to the chin. So it does not allow him to lower his head or to press his nape (*qadhal*), and so he remains *muqmah*. The *muqmah* is one who raises his head and lowers his gaze. It is said: "the camel *qamah*, so he is *qamih*," when it has drunk its fill and raised its head. From this come the two "*shahra qama*h" (the two months of *qama*h, a term for the coldest days of winter), because camels raise their heads from the water on account of its coldness in those two months, and they are the two *kanun*s (the two winter months, Kanun I and II). And from it: "*iqtahamtu al-sawiq*" (I gulped down the barley-porridge).

If you ask: what do you say about the one who makes the pronoun refer to the hands, and claims that since the shackle joins the hand and the neck, and for that reason is called a *jami'a* (a binding), the mention of the necks indicates the mention of the hands? [Mahmud said: If you ask: what do you say about the one who makes the pronoun refer to the hands, and claims that since the shackle joins the hand and the neck, and for that reason is called a *jami'a*, the mention of the necks indicates the mention of the hands. He answered that the correct view is the first one, and he cited this second interpretation with His words ﴿so they are raised-headed﴾, because He made the raising of the head a result of His words ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾. Had the pronoun referred to the hands, the sense of causation in the raising of the heads would not be evident. And [the one who holds it] leaves the clear truth for the confused falsehood. End of his words.] Ahmad said: The *fa'* may be for sequence, like the first *fa'* in His words ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾, or for causation. There is no doubt that the pressing of the hand together with the neck in the shackle necessitates the raising of the head, for the hand, God forbid, remains holding the shackle beneath the chin, pushing it away and preventing it from pressing down. This comparison is more complete on this interpretation, for when the hand is free and unrestrained, the shackled person has some relief through its freedom, and perhaps he may devise by it a way to free himself from the shackle. This is not the case when it is shackled. So, to the separate comparisons we have mentioned, one adds that the closing of the door of stratagems against them, in guidance and in freeing themselves from the noose of disbelief that has been decreed for them, is likened to the shackling of the hands, for the hand is the instrument of resorting to a stratagem for deliverance.

﴿And We made a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them, so they do not see﴾: [I say that] *saddan* (a barrier) is read with the *fath* and the *damm*. It is said: whatever is the work of people is with *fath*, and whatever is the creation of God is with *damm*. ﴿So We covered them﴾: so We covered their sight, that is, We veiled it and placed upon it a covering so that it would not look toward anything seen. According to Mujahid: ﴿We covered them﴾ means: We clothed their sight with a covering. It is also read with the *'ayn* from *al-'asha* (weakness of sight). It is said that it was revealed concerning the clan of Makhzum. Abu Jahl had sworn that if he saw Muhammad (ﷺ) praying, he would crush his head. He came to him while he was praying, with a stone to smash him with. When he raised his hand, it became stuck to his neck and the stone stuck to his hand, until they freed it from him with great difficulty. He returned to his people and informed them. Another man of Makhzum said: "I will kill him with this stone," and he went, and God blinded his eyes. [Ibn Ishaq related it in his *Sirah* in a lengthy account. Abu Nu'aym related it in *al-Dala'il* through Ibn Ishaq: "Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id, or 'Ikrimah, narrated to me, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Abu Jahl said: 'I make a covenant with God that I will sit tomorrow for Muhammad with a stone I cannot lift, and when he prostrates in his prayer I will smash his head with it.'" He mentioned the rest up to his words: "his hands dried up upon his stone," until the stone was hurled between his hands. Then he illustrates their obstinacy in disbelief, and that there is no way for them to be brought back, by making them like those whose necks are shackled and whose heads are raised (*muqmahin*):

In that they do not turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks toward it, nor lower their heads before it. And [they are] like those enclosed between two barriers, unable to see what is before them or behind them: in that they have no reflection and no perception, and that they are blind to contemplating the signs of God. And from it: "*iqtahamtu al-sawiq*" (I gulped down the barley-porridge).

فإن قلت: قد ذكر ما دلّ على انتفاء إيمانهم مع ثبوت الإنذار، ثم قفاه بقوله ﴿إِنَّما تُنْذِرُ﴾ [[قال محمود: «إن قلت: قد ذكر ما دل على انتفاء إيمانهم مع ثبوت الانذار، ثم قفاه بقوله ﴿إِنَّما تُنْذِرُ﴾ وإنما كانت التقفية تصح لو كان الانذار منفيا، وأجاب بأن الأمر كذلك، ولكن لما بين أن البغية المرومة بالإنذار وهي الايمان منفية عنهم: قفاه بقوله ﴿إِنَّما تُنْذِرُ﴾ أى إنما تحصل بغية الانذار ممن اتبع الذكر. انتهى كلامه» قلت: في السؤال سوء أدب، وينبغي أن يقال: وما وجه ذكر الانذار الثاني في معرض المخالفة للأول، مع أن الأول إثبات، والانذار الثاني كذلك.]] وإنما كانت تصح هذه التقفية لو كان الإنذار منفيا. قلت: هو كما قلت، ولكن لما كان ذلك نفيا للايمان مع وجود الإنذار وكان معناه أن البغية المرومة بالإنذار غير حاصلة وهي الإيمان، قفى بقوله ﴿إِنَّما تُنْذِرُ﴾ على معنى: إنما تحصل البغية بإنذارك من غير هؤلاء المنذرين وهم المتبعون للذكر: وهو القرآن أو الوعظ، الخاشون ربهم.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, We bring the dead to life﴾: We resurrect them after their death. It is related from al-Hasan: their giving of life is that He brings them out from polytheism to faith. ﴿And We record what they have sent forward﴾ of good deeds and other deeds, and what they have left behind of good effects, such as knowledge they taught, a book they composed, an endowment (ḥabs) they set aside, or a building they erected: a mosque, a hostel (ribāṭ), a bridge (qanṭara), or the like. Or of evil effects, such as a tax (waẓīfa) that some oppressors imposed on the Muslims, a currency (sikka) through which they introduced cheating (takhsīr) against them, or something new introduced by which people are turned away from the remembrance of God, such as melodies (alḥān) and frivolous amusements (malāhī). Likewise every good or evil practice (sunna) that is followed. A similar statement is His Exalted saying: ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and left behind﴾ [75:13].

That is: what he sent forward of his deeds and left behind of their effects. It has also been said that these are the traces of those who walk to the mosques. It is related from Jabir: We intended to move closer to the mosque, and the open spaces around it were empty, so this reached the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he came to us in our dwellings and said: "O Banu Salama, it has reached me that you intend to move closer to the mosque." We said: "Yes." He said: "Stay in your dwellings, for your traces are being recorded." He said: "So we did not desire to be near the mosque after the Messenger of God ﷺ said that." And it is related from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: "If God were to neglect anything, He would neglect these traces that the winds efface."

Al-Imam: the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ). It is also read: ﴿and their traces are written﴾ with the verb in the passive. And ﴿every thing﴾ is read in the nominative (bi-l-raf').

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, from their saying, "I have of this kind so much," meaning of this example, and these things are of one kind, meaning of one example. The meaning is: strike for them a parable, the likeness of the people of the town. That is, relate to them a wondrous story, the story of the people of the town. The second "parable" (*mathal*) is an explanation of the first.

The *inshāʾ* of *idh* is by its being a *badal* (substitute, apposition) of "the people of the town." The town is Antioch. "The messengers" were the messengers of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) to its people; he sent them as callers to the truth, and the people were worshippers of idols. He sent two of them. When they drew near the city, they saw an old man, Habīb al-Najjār, the companion of Yā-Sīn, tending his little flock. He asked them and they informed him. He said:

"Do you have a sign?" They said: "We heal the sick, and we cure the blind and the leper." He had a son who had been ill for two years, so they wiped over him and he stood up. Habīb believed, and the news spread. Through their hands a great many people were healed. Their account reached the king, and he said to them: "Is there for us a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "I will look into your affair." The people followed them and beat them. It was also said that they were imprisoned. Then ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) sent Shamʿūn, who entered in disguise and mixed with the king's retinue until they became familiar with him. They reported his news to the king, and the king took to him. One day he said to him:

"It has reached me that you imprisoned two men. Have you heard what they are saying?" He said: "No, the state of anger has prevented me from that." So he summoned them. Shamʿūn said: "Who sent you?" They said: "God, who created everything and has no partner." He said: "Describe Him and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and decrees what He desires." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "What the king wishes." So he called for a boy whose eyes were blinded. They called upon God until his sight was split open for him, and they took two pellets and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs by which he could see. Shamʿūn said to him: "Have you seen? If you asked your god until he did the like of this, you would have it, and he would have honour." He said: "I have no secret from you: our god neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Shamʿūn used to enter with them upon the idol, pray, and humble himself, and they thought he was one of them. Then he said:

"If your god is able to bring the dead to life, we will believe in him." So they called for a boy who had died seven days earlier, and he stood up and said: "I was made to enter seven valleys of Fire, and I warn you of what you are in; so believe." And he said: "The gates of heaven were opened and I saw a young man of handsome face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are they?" He said: "Shamʿūn and these two." The king was amazed. When Shamʿūn saw that his words had affected him, he advised him, and he believed, and a people believed with him. Whoever did not believe, Jibrīl (peace be upon him) cried out upon them with a single cry, and they perished. *Fa-ʿazzaznā* means: We strengthened, we reinforced. It is said: "The rain strengthens the earth when it packs and firms it," and "the flesh of the she-camel was firmed." It is also read with the lightening (*takhfīf*), from *ʿazzahu yaʿizzuhu*, meaning: when he overcomes him; that is, *fa-ghalabnā wa-qahharnā* (so We overpowered and subdued) *bi-thālith*, and he was Shamʿūn. If you ask: why was the object omitted? I say: because the purpose is to mention the one by whom strength was given, namely Shamʿūn, and the subtle arrangement in which the truth was exalted and falsehood humbled. When speech is directed toward some purpose, its context and orientation are made for it, as though whatever else is discarded and set aside.

Its parallel is your saying: "The sultan judged today with truth." The purpose toward which the statement is driven is your saying "with truth," so you omitted mention of the one in whose favour and the one against whom the judgment was given. As for *bashar* being in the nominative and *manṣūb* in His saying *mā hādhā basharan* (﴿مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا﴾, "This is not a mortal"): because *illā* (except) nullifies the negation, so the *mā* that resembles *laysa* (*mā al-mushabbaha bi-laysa*) no longer retains resemblance to *laysa*, and so it no longer has government (*ʿamal*). If you ask: why was it said first, ﴿إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ مُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed we are sent to you"), and last, ﴿إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ لَمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed we are surely sent to you" — with the *lām* of emphasis)? I say: because the first is the beginning of information, and the second is a reply to a denial.

They said: "God, who created everything and has no partner." He said: "Describe Him and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and decrees what He desires." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "What the king wishes." So he called for a boy whose eyes were blinded. They called upon God until his sight was split open for him, and they took two pellets and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs by which he could see. Shamʿūn said to him: "Have you seen? If you asked your god until he did the like of this, you would have it, and he would have honour." He said: "I have no secret from you: our god neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Shamʿūn used to enter with them upon the idol, pray, and humble himself, and they thought he was one of them. Then he said:

"If your god is able to bring the dead to life, we will believe in him." So they called for a boy who had died seven days earlier, and he stood up and said: "I was made to enter seven valleys of Fire, and I warn you of what you are in; so believe." And he said: "The gates of heaven were opened and I saw a young man of handsome face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are they?" He said: "Shamʿūn and these two." The king was amazed. When Shamʿūn saw that his words had affected him, he advised him, and he believed, and a people believed with him. Whoever did not believe, Jibrīl (peace be upon him) cried out upon them with a single cry, and they perished. *Fa-ʿazzaznā* means: We strengthened, we reinforced. It is said: "The rain strengthens the earth when it packs and firms it," and "the flesh of the she-camel was firmed." It is also read with the lightening (*takhfīf*), from *ʿazzahu yaʿizzuhu*, meaning: when he overcomes him; that is, *fa-ghalabnā wa-qahharnā* (so We overpowered and subdued) *bi-thālith*, and he was Shamʿūn. If you ask: why was the object omitted? I say: because the purpose is to mention the one by whom strength was given, namely Shamʿūn, and the subtle arrangement in which the truth was exalted and falsehood humbled. When speech is directed toward some purpose, its context and orientation are made for it, as though whatever else is discarded and set aside.

Its parallel is your saying: "The sultan judged today with truth." The purpose toward which the statement is driven is your saying "with truth," so you omitted mention of the one in whose favour and the one against whom the judgment was given. As for *bashar* being in the nominative and *manṣūb* in His saying *mā hādhā basharan* (﴿مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا﴾, "This is not a mortal"): because *illā* (except) nullifies the negation, so the *mā* that resembles *laysa* (*mā al-mushabbaha bi-laysa*) no longer retains resemblance to *laysa*, and so it no longer has government (*ʿamal*). If you ask: why was it said first, ﴿إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ مُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed we are sent to you"), and last, ﴿إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ لَمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed we are surely sent to you" — with the *lām* of emphasis)? I say: because the first is the beginning of information, and the second is a reply to a denial.

[[Note: "I said: how is the phrase 'the nominative and the accusative' of *bashar* in His saying..." — the editor's note: "The expression of al-Nasafi: 'Only the nominative of *bashar* here and the accusative...' etc. (ʿ)."]]

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: why did he omit the *lām* here and affirm it in the second instance, at His saying ﴿رَبُّنَا يَعْلَمُ إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ لَمُرْسَلُونَ﴾? I say: the first is the beginning of information, and the second is a reply to a denial." Ahmad said: i.e., for the sake of emphasis.]]

The phrase "﴿Our Lord knows﴾" functions in the manner of an oath for emphasis (tawkid, "reinforcement"). Likewise, their saying "God bears witness" and "God knows" works the same way. Their answer, which came in the form of emphasis and affirmation, was fitting alongside their statement ﴿And we are only responsible for clear delivery﴾, meaning the manifest and evident [message], made plain by the signs that attest to its truth. Otherwise, if the claimant had said, "By God, I am truthful in what I claim," without bringing forth the proof, it would have been unseemly.

We rejected them and said: "We augur ill from you (tatayyarnā bikum)". Let them be. That was because they disliked their religion and their souls recoiled from it. [[The phrase "ونفرت منهم" is probably "منه" as in the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿAlī)]] It is the habit of the ignorant to take as auspicious everything they incline toward, desire, prefer and that their natures accept, and to take as inauspicious whatever they recoil from and dislike. So if a blessing or a calamity befalls them, they say: "This is by the blessing of such-and-such, and that by the ill omen of such-and-such," as Allah relates of the Copts:

﴿And if an evil befalls them, they augur ill from Moses and those with him.﴾ [Q. 7:131]

And of the polytheists of Makkah:

﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you."﴾ [Q. 7:131]

It was also said that rain was withheld from them, and so they said this. From Qatadah: "If some misfortune befell us, it was because of you." (Tā'irukum maʿakum) ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [Q. 36:19] was also read as "ṭayrukum", meaning: the cause of your ill omen is with you, which is your disbelief. Or: the causes of your ill omen are with you, which are your disbelief and your sins. Al-Hasan read "aṭayrukum", meaning "your augury (taṭayyur)". It was also read "a-in dhakkartum?" with the interrogative hamzah and the conditional particle; and "ā'in" with an alif between them, [[The text in al-Nasafi indicates that this and what precedes it have a kasrah-marked yā' in place of the second hamzah. (ʿAlī)]] meaning: "Do you augur ill if you are reminded?" It was also read "a-anna dhakkartum?" with the interrogative hamzah and the subordinating "anna", meaning: "Did you augur ill because you were reminded?" It was read "anna" and "inna" without interrogation, in the sense of a statement, meaning: "You augured ill because you were reminded," or "If you are reminded, you augur ill." It was also read "ayna dhakkartum" with lightening (al-takhfīf), meaning: your ill omen is with you wherever your reminder has taken place; and when a place is made ill-omened by their mention, then their dwelling in it is more ill-omened.

﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed the bounds﴾ [Q. 36:19] in disobedience. Therefore the misfortune has come to you, not from the messengers of Allah and their admonition; or: "Nay, you are a people who exceed the bounds in your misguidance, persisting in your error, in that you augur ill from those whom it is obligatory to seek blessing from: the messengers of Allah."

A man came running from the farthest part of the city. He was Habib ibn Israil al-Najjar, who used to carve idols. He believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and there were six hundred years between them, just as Tubba' al-Akbar and Waraqah ibn Nawfal and others believed in him. No one believed in a prophet except after his appearance. It is also said that he was in a cave worshipping Allah, and when news of the messengers reached him, he came to them, made his religion manifest, and debated with the disbelievers. They said, "Do you oppose our religion?" and they rushed upon him and killed him.

It is also said that they trampled him with their feet until his intestines (al-qasab) came out from his rear. The lexicographers say that al-qasab, in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), means the intestines, and al-ma'a is the singular of al-am'a (intestines). It is also said that they stoned him while he was saying, "O Allah, guide my people." His grave is in the market of Antioch. When he was killed, Allah became angry with them, and they were destroyed by the cry of Jibril (peace be upon him).

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The foremost of the nations are three: those who did not disbelieve in Allah for the blink of an eye: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the companion of Ya-Sin, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh." [Al-Tha'labi narrated it through the chain of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla from his father with this wording, and in it is Amr ibn Jami', who is abandoned (matruk) in narration. Al-Uqayli, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through the chain of Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Ashqar from Ibn Uyayna from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, with the wording: "The foremost are three: the one who was foremost to Isa is the companion of Ya-Sin, and the one foremost to Muhammad (ﷺ) is Ali ibn Abi Talib."]

﴿Follow those who ask no reward of you, and who are rightly guided.﴾ This is a comprehensive phrase encouraging them to follow such people, meaning: you will lose nothing of your worldly wealth with them, and you will gain the soundness of your religion, so that the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter come together for you. Then he presented his words in the form of advising himself, while he intended to advise them, so that he would be gentle with them and tolerant towards them. This is also more effective in sincere advice, since he wanted for them only what he wanted for himself. He placed his words ﴿And why should I not worship the One who created me?﴾ in place of ﴿And why should you not worship the One who created you?﴾ Do you not see his words ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾? Had he not intended this, he would have said, "the One who created me, and to whom I will return." He drove the speech in this direction until he said ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾, meaning: listen to my word and obey me. I have warned you of the sound truth from which there is no deviation: that worship is valid only for the One from whom your origin is and to whom your return is. How repugnant and detestable it is to me that you would prefer to worship things that, if He (the Most Merciful) intends harm for you, these would not be able to intercede for you, their intercession would not benefit you, they would not be permitted to be intercessors before Him, and they could not rescue you from Him in any way whatsoever. Indeed, in this preference you are falling into manifest error that is not hidden from anyone of intellect and discernment.

It is also said: when he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hurried towards the messengers before he was killed, and said to them, ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾, meaning: listen to my faith, so that you may bear witness to it on my behalf.

It is recited (qari'a, a variant recitation): "in yuridni al-Rahman bi-durr," with the meaning "an yuriduni durran," that is, to make me one who is exposed to harm (﴿if the Most Merciful wills harm for me﴾).

This is also more effective in sincere advice, since he wanted for them only what he wanted for himself. He placed his words ﴿And why should I not worship the One who created me?﴾ in place of ﴿And why should you not worship the One who created you?﴾ Do you not see his words ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾? Had he not intended this, he would have said, "the One who created me, and to whom I will return." He drove the speech in this direction until he said ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾, meaning: listen to my word and obey me. I have warned you of the sound truth from which there is no deviation: that worship is valid only for the One from whom your origin is and to whom your return is. Indeed, in this preference you are falling into manifest error that is not hidden from anyone of intellect and discernment.

A man came running from the farthest part of the city. He was Habib ibn Israil al-Najjar, who used to carve idols. He believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and there were six hundred years between them, just as Tubba' al-Akbar and Waraqah ibn Nawfal and others believed in him. No one believed in a prophet except after his appearance. It is also said that he was in a cave worshipping Allah, and when news of the messengers reached him, he came to them, made his religion manifest, and debated with the disbelievers. They said, "Do you oppose our religion?" and they rushed upon him and killed him.

It is also said that they trampled him with their feet until his intestines (al-qasab) came out from his rear. The lexicographers say that al-qasab, in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), means the intestines, and al-ma'a is the singular of al-am'a (intestines). It is also said that they stoned him while he was saying, "O Allah, guide my people." His grave is in the market of Antioch. When he was killed, Allah became angry with them, and they were destroyed by the cry of Jibril (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verses 26–27:

That is, when he was killed, it was said to him: ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ And it is related from Qatadah: God admitted him into Paradise, and he is in it alive, being provided for, and he meant the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Nay, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for, rejoicing﴾. And it has been said: its meaning is the glad tidings of entering Paradise and that he is among its people. If you ask: how is this statement classified in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-bayan)? I answer: it is classified as a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf), because this is a place where one would ask about his condition at meeting his Lord. As if a questioner said: how was his meeting with his Lord after that steadfastness in supporting his religion and offering his soul sincerely for His sake? So it was said: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾, and it did not say "it was said to him," because the aim is directed to the words spoken and their magnitude, not to the one addressed, although he is known. Likewise, his saying ﴿Would that my people knew﴾ is arranged on the presumption of a questioner asking about what he experienced at that moment of great triumph. He only wished that his people knew his condition, so that their knowledge of it would be a cause for them to acquire the like for themselves, by repenting of disbelief and entering faith and righteous deeds, which lead their people to Paradise. And in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): he advised his people while alive and dead.[[This appears in the story of ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from a hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah, mentioning the story, and at its end: "He kept saying, while in the throes of death: O people of Thaqif, come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and ask him for safety before my death reaches him, lest he attack you." He continued like this until he died, and it reached the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "He advised his people, in life and in death," and his likeness is that of the companion of Yasin.]] In it is a great admonition on the obligation to restrain anger, to show forbearance toward the ignorant, to be compassionate toward one who has entered among the wicked and the rebellious, to strive earnestly to rescue him and to be gentle in ransoming him, and to occupy oneself with that rather than with gloating over him or invoking curses upon him. Do you not see how he wished good for his killers and for those who plotted evil against him, though they were disbelievers and idol-worshippers? It is also permissible that he wished this so that they would know they had been in great error regarding his affair, and that he had been upon rightness, sincere advice and compassion, and that their enmity had brought him nothing but triumph and had been followed by nothing but felicity, since that increases his delight and multiplies his joy and happiness. The first is more apt. It has been read: ﴿al-mukarrimin﴾ (the honored). If you ask: what is in His saying ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾, which mā is it? I answer: it is either the verbal-source mā (al-māʾ al-maṣdariyyah) or the relative mā (al-māʾ al-mawṣulah), meaning: with that which He forgave me of sins. It may also be interrogative, meaning: with what thing my Lord forgave me, intending by it what he had done with them of perseverance in exalting the religion until he was killed. However, your saying "bimā ghafara lī" with the alif dropped is better, though keeping it is permissible. It is said: "I know what you did with this" (qad ʿalimtu bimā ṣanaʿta hādhā), meaning: with what thing did you do it, and with what did you do it.

**Meaning:** God sufficed to deal with their affair by a single cry from an angel. He did not send down to destroy them any host from the hosts of heaven, as He did on the day of Badr and the Trench (al-Khandaq).

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾? I say its meaning is:

It was not fitting in Our wisdom to send down against the people of the messenger (Habib) a host from heaven to destroy them. This is because God, exalted is He, has ordained the destruction of each people in some ways and not others, and this is only based on what wisdom requires and what benefit necessitates. Do you not see His words, ﴿So of them We sent against some a storm of stones, and of them some were seized by the Cry, and of them some We caused the earth to swallow, and of them some We drowned﴾?

If you ask: then why were hosts sent down from heaven on the day of Badr and the Trench? He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾, ﴿with a thousand angels following one another﴾, ﴿with three thousand angels sent down﴾, ﴿with five thousand angels marked﴾?

I say: only one angel would have sufficed. The cities of the people of Lot were overturned with a feather from the wing of Gabriel, and the lands of Thamud and the people of Salih were destroyed by a cry from him. But God favoured Muhammad (ﷺ) in every respect over the great prophets and the steadfast messengers (ulu al-'azm), and far beyond Habib al-Najjar and his like, granting him, among the causes of honour and of excuse, what He granted no one else. Among that: He sent down hosts for him from heaven. It is as if He indicated, with His words ﴿And We did not send down, and We were not going to send down﴾, that sending down hosts is among the great matters for which only one like you is qualified, and that We would not do with anyone else what We did for you.

﴿It was but a single cry﴾: that is, if the seizing or the punishment was only a single cry. Abu Ja'far al-Madani read it with the nominative (raf'), taking kana as the complete verb (kan al-tamma, "was/occurred"), meaning: "there occurred only a cry." Analogy and usage require the verb to be masculine, since the meaning is: "nothing occurred except a cry." But he looked to the apparent form of the word, and the cry is treated as the agent of the verb. Similar is the reading of al-Hasan: ﴿So they became such that none was seen except their dwellings﴾, and the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"Its flesh was wasted by the journey through the deserts and their heat,
and there remained only the ribs, the heaving ones."*

It is by Labid, describing his she-camel: that the journey through the barren lands wasted her flesh, meaning the travel in them and their fierce heat, and there remained in her only the ribs. The more eloquent form would have been to drop the feminine ta', since the meaning is: "nothing remained in it except the ribs," but he made it feminine in view of the ribs (al-dulu'). Al-Jarashi'(a): plural of jarshi', like qunfudh, meaning thick and prominent. It is also transmitted with a different first hemistich:

*"The heat and the barren stretches folded up what was in their flanks."*

Al-ajraz: plural of jarz, meaning the barren wasteland. Al-'urud: plural of 'arad (with a damma and sukun), meaning its sides. It is also transmitted with al-nahz in place of al-harr: that is with a nun, then an unpointed ha', then a zay, meaning goading and pushing. It is also transmitted as "ghurud" with a dotted ghayn, plural of ghars, like qufl, meaning the girth-strap of the saddle; he meant by it the chest, by association of contiguity. Or it is by omission of a noun, meaning the place of its ghurud. It is permissible that he meant by "what is in its ghurud" the chest itself, not the fat and flesh. The meaning of tay (folding) is emaciation, or removal, used figuratively.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿al-azqiyah﴾ (as a single cry, wahidah), from zaqa al-tair, yazqu and yazqa, when it cries out. From it is the proverb: "heavier than the zawaqi" (the cry of birds). ﴿Khamidun﴾ means they were extinguished as fire is extinguished, becoming ashes, as Labid said:

*"The man is nothing but like a spark and its light,
it turns to ash after it was blazing.
And wealth and family are nothing but deposits,
and the deposits must one day be returned."*

By Labid al-'Amiri. That is: the state of a man, his life, his splendour, then his death and annihilation after that, is nothing but like the state of a spark of fire and its light, in that it becomes ash after its illumination. It is possible that his words "turns to ash" are a resumed sentence (isti'naf) explaining the aspect of the comparison, which is a comparison of state (tashbih hay'a). It is not correct to compare the man himself with the spark and its light. He compared the wealth of a person and his relatives to deposits, an eloquent comparison, in that all must be taken back. He explained this with his words: "and deposits must one day be returned."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verse 30:

"Alas for the servants!" This is an address to the regret ("hasra") concerning them, as if it were said to it: "Come, O regret, for this is among your states, in which it is your right to be present," and this state is their mockery of the messengers. The meaning is that they are deserving that those who feel regret should feel regret over them, and that those who grieve over their condition should grieve. Or it may be that the one who feels regret over them is from the standpoint of the angels and the believers among the two species (humans and jinn). It is also permissible that it comes from God, may He be exalted, by way of metaphor, in the sense of magnifying what they committed against themselves and brought upon themselves, and His extreme disapproval of it and His wonder at it. The reading of one who reads "Alas, my regret!" (yā ḥasratā) supports this interpretation, since the meaning is "O my regret!" It has also been read "Yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" (O regret of the servants), with the genitive linking it to them, because the regret is specific to them, in that it is directed at them. And "yā ḥasratun ʿalā al-ʿibād" is by applying the pause form to the continuous reading.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verses 31–32:

أَلَمْ يَرَوْا: "alam yaʿlamū" (did they not know). It is suspended from operating on كَمْ (kam, "how many"), because كَمْ is not governed by any operator that precedes it. It is interrogative or declarative, since its origin is interrogative. However, its meaning extends over the whole clause, as it did in your saying: "Did you not see that Zayd is surely going?" Even though it does not govern the form of the word (inna, "surely," which is not affected).

وَأَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ لا يَرْجِعُونَ: this is a substitute (badal) for كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا ("how many We destroyed"), in meaning and not in form. Its sense is: "Did they not see the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they would not return to them?"

It is reported from al-Hasan that he read إنّ with a kasra, as a new resumed sentence (istinaf).

In the reading of Ibn Masʿud, "أَلَمْ يَرَوْا مَنْ أَهْلَكْنا" (did they not see whom We destroyed), the substitution in this reading is a badal ishtimal (inclusive substitution). This refutes the view of the people of al-Rajʿah (the belief in the return of certain dead persons before the Resurrection).

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he was told: "Some people claim that ʿAli will be sent back before the Day of Resurrection." He said: "Evil is the people, then, we would have married his wives and divided his inheritance." [[Reported by al-Hakim in his commentary on Surat al-Baqarah in a similar form, abridged. He also reported it from the hadith of al-Hasan in the Virtues of the Companions, in a more complete form.

The phrase "Evil is the people, then" is not in it.]]

Lamma is read with a light (takhfif) pronunciation, where the مَا is an extra particle for emphasis (silah lil-taʾkid), and إنْ is a lightened form of the heavy inna, which is necessarily followed by the lam. Lamma with a heavy (tashdid) pronunciation means "except" (illa), like the one in the matter of the Book: "I adjure you by Allah, did you do it?" and إنْ is a negative particle.

The tanwin in كُلٌّ is what stands as a replacement (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun that follows it, as in your saying: "I passed by everyone standing." The meaning is that all of them are gathered, assembled, and brought forth for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. It is said that "muhdarun" means they are brought forth to be punished.

If you ask: how is كل described by جميع when their meaning is the same? I answer: they are not the same, because كلا conveys the sense of encompassing, that not one of them escapes, while جميع conveys the sense of collectivity, that the gathering place assembles them. جميع is a form of فعيل in the sense of مفعول (passive), as in "ḥayyun jamīʿ" (a living people gathered together) and "jāʾū jamīʿan" (they came all together).

وَأَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ لا يَرْجِعُونَ: this is a substitute (badal) for كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا ("how many We destroyed"), in meaning and not in form. Its sense is: "Did they not see the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they would not return to them?"

It is reported from al-Hasan that he read إنّ with a kasra, as a new resumed sentence (istinaf).

In the reading of Ibn Masʿud, "أَلَمْ يَرَوْا مَنْ أَهْلَكْنا" (did they not see whom We destroyed), the substitution in this reading is a badal ishtimal (inclusive substitution). This refutes the view of the people of al-Rajʿah (the belief in the return of certain dead persons before the Resurrection).

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he was told: "Some people claim that ʿAli will be sent back before the Day of Resurrection." He said: "Evil is the people, then, we would have married his wives and divided his inheritance." [[Reported by al-Hakim in his commentary on Surat al-Baqarah in a similar form, abridged. He also reported it from the hadith of al-Hasan in the Virtues of the Companions, in a more complete form.

The phrase "Evil is the people, then" is not in it.]]

Lamma is read with a light (takhfif) pronunciation, where the مَا is an extra particle for emphasis (silah lil-taʾkid), and إنْ is a lightened form of the heavy inna, which is necessarily followed by the lam. Lamma with a heavy (tashdid) pronunciation means "except" (illa), like the one in the matter of the Book: "I adjure you by Allah, did you do it?" and إنْ is a negative particle.

The tanwin in كُلٌّ is what stands as a replacement (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun that follows it, as in your saying: "I passed by everyone standing." The meaning is that all of them are gathered, assembled, and brought forth for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. It is said that "muhdarun" means they are brought forth to be punished.

If you ask: how is كل described by جميع when their meaning is the same? I answer: they are not the same, because كلا conveys the sense of encompassing, that not one of them escapes, while جميع conveys the sense of collectivity, that the gathering place assembles them. جميع is a form of فعيل in the sense of مفعول (passive), as in "ḥayyun jamīʿ" (a living people gathered together) and "jāʾū jamīʿan" (they came all together).

The recitation ﴿bi-l-mayyita﴾ with a light pronunciation (*takhfif*) is more common, because it flows easily on the tongue. ﴿Wa-ahyaynaha﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that explains), clarifying why the dead earth is a sign. The same applies to ﴿naslakh﴾. It is permissible for the earth and the night to be described by a verb, because both are intended as general categories (*jinsan*), not as specific earth or specific night.

[[Mahmud said: "It is permissible for ﴿ahyaynaha﴾ to be an attributive description of the earth, and this is valid because the intended 'earth' is a category, not a particular earth. It may also be an explanation of the aspect of the sign in it." Ahmad said: Other grammarians prohibit a sentence from functioning as an attribute of a definite noun, even if that noun is generic and not specific in meaning. This prohibition observes lexical agreement in attributive use, as in:

"And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me."]]

But they are treated as indefinite nouns in their description by verbs, as in the line:

"And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me." [[The explanation of this witness was given earlier, in the first part, page 16; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

His words ﴿fa-minhu ya'kulun﴾ place the adverbial phrase first, to indicate that grain is the thing on which most of life depends, and on which human welfare rests through sustenance. When it decreases, famine comes and harm occurs; when it is lost, destruction comes and calamity descends.

﴿Wa-fajjarna﴾ is read both with light and heavy stress; *al-fajr* and *al-tafjir* are like *al-fath* and *al-tafth*, in both wording and meaning.

﴿Thamarihi﴾ is read with two fathas, with two dammas, with a damma and a sukun. The pronoun refers to God, Exalted. The meaning is: that they may eat of what God created of the fruit, ﴿wa-mimma 'amilat-hu aydihim﴾ ("and of what their hands made") through planting, irrigation, wells, and other labours, until the fruit reached its term and the time of its eating. The meaning is that the fruit in itself is God's act and creation, yet it bears the traces of human toil. Its original form was "from *thamarina*" as in ﴿wa-ja'alna﴾ and ﴿wa-fajjarna﴾, so the speech shifts from first person to third person, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person). It is permissible for the pronoun to refer to the palm trees, leaving the grapes without a referent, since it is known that they share the status of palm trees regarding the eating of their fruit. It is also permissible for it to refer to the previously mentioned fruit, which is the gardens, as Ru'ba said:

"In them are streaks of white and spots, as if on the hide the pattern of white leprosy..."

[[The explanation of this witness was given earlier, in the first part, page 149; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

He was asked about this and said: "I meant 'as if that.'" You may also make *ma* a negation, so that the meaning is that the fruit is God's creation and human hands did not make it, nor are they able to do so. It has been read in the first way, with ﴿wa-ma 'amilat﴾ without a returning pronoun, and this is how it appears in the codices of the people of Kufa; in the codices of the people of the Two Sanctuaries, Basra and Syria, it appears with the pronoun.

﴿Al-azwaj﴾ means kinds and categories. ﴿Wa-mimma la ya'lamun﴾ means: of kinds that God has not made known to them, and they have no means of knowing through any path of knowledge. It is not unlikely that God creates among creatures animals and inanimate things for which He has not provided humanity a way to knowledge, since they have no need of that knowledge in their religion or their worldly affairs. Had they needed it, He would have informed them of what they do not know, just as He informed them of the existence of what they do not know.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "He did not name them." And in a hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, let alone what I have revealed to them." So He informed us of its existence and preparation but did not tell us what it is, similar to ﴿fa-la ta'lamu nafsun ma ukhfiya lahum min qurrati a'yun﴾. In informing us of the abundance of what He created, both what they know and what they do not know, there is evidence of the greatness of His power and the vastness of His dominion.

Skinning a sheep: when one strips the hide off it and removes it. From this comes the shedding of a snake's skin (al-kharshā’) — so the word is borrowed for the removal of light and its uncovering from the place of the night and where its shadow falls: ﴿مُظْلِمُونَ﴾ meaning they enter into darkness. It is said: "aẓlamnā" (we entered darkness), just as you say "a'tamnā" (we entered the night's late hours) and "adjaynā" (we entered the dark of night).

﴿لِمُسْتَقَرٍّ لَّهَا﴾ — for a fixed resting place of its own: a predetermined, appointed limit at which it comes to rest in its orbit at the end of the year. It is likened to the resting place of a traveller when he has finished his journey. Or it means: for a limit of its own among the risings and the settings, since it traces them out, rising point by rising point and setting point by setting point, until it reaches its furthest point, then returns; that is its limit and resting place, since it does not go beyond it. Or it means: a limit of its own in its course each day within our sight, which is the setting.

It is also said: its resting place is its appointed term, which God fixed for its course, so it settles upon it, and that is the end of the year. And it is said: it is the time at which it comes to rest and its motion ceases, and that is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verses 38–40:

It is read: "tajri ila mustaqarr lahā" (it runs toward its resting place). Ibn Mas'ud read: "lā mustaqarra lahā," meaning: it never ceases running and never comes to rest. It is also read: "lā mustaqarr lahā," where lā is taken in the sense of laysa (is not): that running is not upon that measure and that precise calculation, which the keen-minded are unable to extract and whose derivation the intellects are bewildered by. It is nothing but the measuring of the Mighty, who has power over every thing that can be done, and who encompasses every knowable thing in knowledge.

It is read: "wa-l-qamaru" in the nominative (rafʿan), as a new subject (ibtidāʾ), or in the genitive as a conjunction with "al-layl" (ʿaṭfan ʿalā al-layl). The meaning is: among His signs is the moon. It is also read in the accusative (naṣban), governed by a verb that the phrase "qaddarnāhu" explains. In "qaddarnāhu manāzila" there must be an elided genitive-governing noun (taqdīr muḍāf), because it makes no sense to say that the moon itself is measured as stations. The meaning is: We measured its course as stations, and they are twenty-eight stations. The moon descends in one of them every night, not passing beyond it and not falling short of it, according to a measure that is even and does not vary. It travels through them each night from the beginning of the month to the twenty-eighth, then it is hidden for two nights or one night when the month is deficient. These stations are the positions of the stars to which the Arabs attributed the rain-bringing seasonal risings (al-anwāʾ al-mustamṭira). They are: al-Sharatān, al-Baṭīn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwāʾ, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Balda, Saʿd al-Dhābih, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farʿ al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farʿ al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and al-Rishāʾ. When it reaches the last of its stations, it becomes thin and curved, and returns "like the old date-stalk," ʿurjūn (ʿurjūn al-qadīm), which is the stalk of the palm cluster, the part between its spikelets and its point of origin on the palm tree. Al-Zajjaj said: it is "fuʿlūn" from al-inʿirāj, which is bending. It is also read "al-ʿirjūn," on the pattern of "al-firjūn" [[His words "wa-qurʾa al-ʿirjūn bi-wazn al-firjūn": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-firjūn" is the ... ]], and both are dialectal forms, like "al-bazyūn" and "al-buzyūn." The "old" (qadīm) is that which has passed a year, and when it is old it becomes dry, bends, and turns yellow, so it is compared to it in three respects. It was said: the minimum period for something described as old is one year. So if a man says, "Every slave of mine who is old is free," or writes in his will, "Free from among them those who have spent a year or more," [the year applies].

It is read: "sābiq al-nahār," in accordance with the original form. The meaning is that God Most High apportioned to each of the night and the day and their two signs a portion of time, set for each a known limit, and arranged their affairs in alternation. So it is not appropriate for the sun, that is, it is not easy for it, nor proper, nor does it stand right, since the arrangement falls upon alternation. Even if each of the two luminaries is given authority in its own domain [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is that each of them does not enter upon the other's authority so as to extinguish its light; rather they alternate according to His arrangement. He said: If you ask, why did you make the sun not overtaking and the moon not preceding? I say: because the sun moves slowly, completing its orbit in a year, while the moon completes its orbit in a month, so the sun, by its slowness, is worthy of being described as overtaking, and the moon, by its swiftness, is worthy of being described as preceding. End of his words." Ahmad said: From this verse it is derived that the day follows the night, which is the well-known position of the jurists. Its explanation from the verse is that He made the sun, which is the sign of the day, not overtaking the moon, which is the sign of the night. He negated overtaking because it is what can occur, and that requires the moon to precede and the sun to follow, for one does not say "the preceding overtook the following," but "the following overtook the preceding." By what is possible, the negation is phrased accordingly. So the night is the one followed, and the day is the follower.

If it is said: Does this imply that the night precedes the day? The verse explicitly says it does not precede. The answer: this objection is shared. The probable divisions are three: either the day follows the night, which is the view of the jurists; or the reverse, which is reported from a group of grammarians; or their coming together, and this third division is negated by consensus. Nothing remains but the day following the night and its reverse. This objection applies to both of them, for whoever says the day precedes the night is bound to hold that the rhetorical form would have been: "nor does the night overtake the day," for when the later one's overtaking is negated, that is more eloquent than negating its preceding, while it diverges from the sense of His words "lā al-shamsu yanbaghī lahā an tudrika al-qamar," a divergence that does not gather the meaning together with the wording. For God negated that it be overtaking, let alone preceding. Having established this, the well-founded answer is that what is negated is the preceding that entails the day's lagging behind the night and an interval of time between them; then alternation is established, which is what the verse intends. As for the first of two alternating things preceding the other, it is not considered. Do you not see Moses' answer with His words, "They are on my track"? He made light of their lateness by saying they were following his track, so how would it be if he had been ahead while they were behind with no distance between them and him? Had that occurred, the context of the verse would require that it not be counted as haste or preceding. Then saying the day precedes the night contradicts the beginning of the verse in a way that admits no interpretation, for between the negation of overtaking, which indicates delay and following, and the statement of preceding, there is a great gap, and it also contradicts the rest of the verse. If the night were following and later, it would be more fitting to describe it as not overtaking, without going so far as to negate preceding; and the claim that the night precedes the day would match the beginning of the verse explicitly, and would be consistent with the structure of the Qur'an by some interpretation. The proof of its opposite is closer to truth than a vein in the neck. Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 36, verses 41–44:

"Their offspring" (dhurriyyatahum): their children and those whose burden concerns them. It was also said: the term dhurriyyah applies to women, since they are its cultivators (mazari'uha). And in a hadith, he (ﷺ) forbade killing the dhurriyy, meaning the women.

"And the like of it" (min mithlihi): from the likeness of the ship (al-Fulk), "that they ride" (ma yarkabun): camels, which are the ships of the land.

It was also said: al-Fulk al-mashhun is the ship of Noah. The meaning of God carrying "their offspring" in it is that He carried in it their forefathers, and in their loins were they and their offspring. He mentioned their offspring rather than them because it is more eloquent in bestowing favour upon them and more effective in marveling at His power, in carrying their descendants until the Day of Resurrection in the ship of Noah.

"And the like of it" (min mithlihi): from the like of that ship, namely the ships and boats that they ride.

"Then there is no outcry" (fala sarikha): no one to rescue them. That is, there is no help (ighathah). It is said: "The one crying out for help came to them" (atahumu al-sarikh).

"Nor are they rescued" (wa la hum yunqadhun): they are not saved from death by drowning.

"Except as a mercy" (illa rahmatan): except by a mercy from Us, "and as enjoyment of life" (wa litamti'an) "for a time" (ila hin): until an appointed term in which they will die, as they must, after being saved from drowning.

[Ahmad says: From here Abu al-Tayyib took:

"I was not saved so that I might remain, but I was saved from one death-bath only to reach another."

For He, exalted is He, informed that if they are saved from death by drowning, that safety is a provision for a time, meaning until a term at which they will die, and there is no escape.]

And well did the one who said:

"I was not saved so that I might remain, but I was saved from one death-bath only to reach another."

[Al-Mutanabbi says: I was not saved from the calamities of time and the hardships of war in order to live forever; rather, I was saved from death by some causes until I die by others. Or: I am returning to death by others, for there is no immortality in this world.]

Al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "nughriqahum" (We drown them).

﴿Beware of what is before you and what is behind you﴾, like His saying: ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and what is behind them of the heaven and the earth?﴾ And from Mujahid: what has preceded of your sins and what has come after. Then he said:

"Their habit is turning away at every sign and admonition."

The zindiqs among them would hear the believers attribute God's actions to His will, and they would say: "If God willed, He would make so-and-so rich; if He willed, He would make him mighty; if He willed, it would be such-and-such." They gave this reply in the manner of mockery toward the believers and toward what they used to say about attaching matters to God's will. Its meaning is: "Shall we feed the one of whom you speak this speech among you?" That is because they used to deny that wealth and poverty come from God, for they were mu'attilah (deniers of divine attributes), who did not believe in the Creator.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that there were zindiqs in Makkah, and when they were commanded to give charity to the needy, they said: "No, by Allah! Shall God impoverish him and we feed him?"

It has also been said: they were giving the impression that God, Exalted is He, was able to feed him but did not will to feed him, so we have more right to that. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh when the poor companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give us from what you claim from your wealth is for Allah," meaning His saying: ﴿And they assign to Allah a share of what He has produced of the tilth and the cattle﴾ [al-An'am 6:136]. So they denied them, and said: "If Allah willed, He would feed you."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verse 48–50:

"You are only in manifest error" (﴿إِنْ أَنْتُمْ إِلَّا فِي ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾) is either the words of God addressed to them, or the recounting of the words of the believers to them, or it is part of their answer to the believers.

It has been read as wa-hum yakhsimūn (وهم يخصمون), with the tā' assimilated into the ṣād (idghām), with the kha' vowelled both as fatḥa and as kasra, and with the yā' of the verb following the kha' in its kasra (ittibā'). It has also been read as yakhtaṣimūn (يختصمون), in its original form, and as yakhsimūn, from khaṣamahu (خصمه).

The meaning is: the Hour will seize them while they are in their security and heedlessness of it, not bringing it to mind, occupied with their disputes in their trade, their dealings, and all the other matters about which they quarrel and wrangle.

The meaning of khaṣimūn is: some of them dispute with others. It has also been said: it will seize them while they are, in their own estimation, disputing in argument about whether they will be resurrected. ﴿فَلا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ تَوْصِيَةً﴾ ("so they will not be able to make any bequest") concerning any of their affairs, and ﴿وَلا إِلَى أَهْلِهِمْ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ ("nor will they be able to return to their households") to their homes and families. Rather, they will die exactly where the Blast overtakes them.

It is read ﴿الصُّورِ﴾ with a sukun on the waw, meaning the horn, or as the plural of ṣūrah (form). Some read it with a vowel on the waw. Al-ajdāth means the graves. It is also read with a fā᾽ instead of the thā᾽, as al-ajdāf (see al-Sihah, the lexicon: "al-jadf" means the grave, and it is a substitution for al-jadth). Al-Farrā᾽ said: "The Arabs alternate between fā᾽ and thā᾽ in speech, so they say jadth and jadf, and the plurals are al-ajdāth and al-ajdāf." ﴿يَنْسِلُونَ﴾ means they run quickly. It is read with a kasra or a ḍamma on the sīn. This is the second blast.

It is read: ﴿يا ويلتنا﴾ ("O woe to us!"). It is also reported from Ibn Mas῾ūd, may Allah be pleased with him: "min ahabanā" (who roused us), from habba min nawmihi, meaning he woke up, and ahabahu meaning someone else woke him. It is also read: "min habbanā," in the sense of ahabanā. It is reported from some of them that he intended habba bina, deleting the preposition and making the verb transitive.

It is also read: "min ba῾thinā" and "min habbanā," with min as the preposition and the noun as a verbal noun. Here, hādhā is the subject (mubtada᾽), and mā waʿada is its predicate. Mā is either a verbal (maṣdariyyah) or a relative (mawṣūlah) particle. It is also permissible for hādhā to be an adjective of al-marqad, and mā waʿada to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is what the Most Merciful promised," so that the subject is omitted and the predicate is the one mentioned. ﴿وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ means the truth. It is reported from Mujāhid: the disbelievers have a brief sleep in which they taste the pleasure of sleep. When the people of the graves are called, they say, "Who has roused us?" As for "This is what the Most Merciful promised," it is the speech of the angels, reported from Ibn ῾Abbās. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: it is the speech of the righteous. It is also said: it is the speech of the disbelievers, recalling what they heard from the messengers, and they answer it themselves or one another.

If you ask: if you make mā a verbal particle, the meaning is "This is what the Most Merciful promised and what the messengers spoke truly," by naming the promised thing and the truthful thing as the promise and the truth. What is the meaning of ﴿وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ if you make it a relative particle? I answer: its implied sense is "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and what the messengers affirmed as true," meaning: "And what the messengers spoke truly about." This comes from their saying "ṣaddaqūhum al-ḥadīth" and "al-qitāl" (they confirmed the report and the fighting to them), and from it: "ṣadaqanī sinn bakrah" (the young camel's tooth confirmed me).

If you ask: "Who has roused us from our resting place?" is a question about the one who raises them, so how does this answer correspond to it? I answer: its meaning is that the Most Merciful, who promised you resurrection and whom the messengers informed you of, has raised you. But it has come in the manner of: "their hearts were made to hear evil tidings, their conditions were announced to them, their disbelief and denial were mentioned, and they were told of the occurrence of what they were warned about." It is as if they were told: "This is not the resurrection you know, which is the resurrection of a sleeper from his bed, so that the question of who raises you should concern you. Rather, this is the greatest resurrection, full of terrors and fears, and it is what Allah promised in His books revealed upon the tongues of His truthful messengers."

﴿Except a single blast﴾, read in the accusative and in the nominative. ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ ... ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in occupation﴾. [Ahmad said: Here the indefiniteness of ﴿شغل﴾ (shughl, "occupation") is for magnification, as if it were said: "in an occupation", meaning an occupation of a kind beyond description. Likewise the verse ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾.] This is a report of what will be said to them on that Day. In such a report there is an added depiction of the promised reward, its firm establishment in the souls, and an encouragement to strive for it and for what it yields. ﴿In occupation﴾: in what kind of occupation? An indescribable occupation. And consider the occupation of one who has been made happy by entering the Garden, which is the abode of the God-fearing, who has reached the attainment of that felicity and that great dominion and lasting bliss, and has fallen into those delights which Allah has prepared for His chosen servants, as a recompense for their deeds, together with honour and exaltation. This comes after the longing and yearning, and after being freed from the hardships of obligation and the narrow passes of piety and fear, and after passing over the terrors, crossing the dangers, and traversing the Bridge (al-Sirat). It also comes after witnessing what the sinners suffered of punishment.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: [the occupation is] in the deflowering of virgins.

And from him: [it is] in the striking of the lutes. From Ibn Kaysan: [it is] in mutual visiting. It was said: [it is] in the hospitality of Allah. From al-Hasan: [it is] that what the people of the Fire are in has preoccupied them with enjoying what they have. From al-Kalbi: they are occupied, away from their families among the people of the Fire, so that their affair does not concern them and they do not remember them, lest any disturbance enter into their bliss.

It was read: ﴿fi shughul﴾ with two dammas, with a damma and a sukun, with two fathas, and with a fatha and a sukun. [The words] al-fakih and al-fikih mean one who is luxuriating and one who is delighting in pleasures, and from it comes al-fakiha (fruit), because it is something one delights in. Likewise al-fukaha (jesting), which is joking. It was read ﴿fakihun﴾ and ﴿fikihun﴾, with kasra and damma of the kaf, as in the saying: "rajul hadath" and "hadath" (a man who is good in speech), and "nutus" and "nutus" (one who is extreme in purification and precise in knowledge). [Footnote: "as in the saying 'rajul hadath' means one good in conversation, and 'nutus' means one who is extreme in purity and precise in knowledge; as stated in al-Sihah." (ʿAyn)]

It was read: ﴿fakihina﴾ and ﴿fikihina﴾, on the basis that it is a circumstantial state (hal, a state accusative).

The adverbial phrase ﴿hum﴾ may be the subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), or it may be an emphasis (ta'kid) of the pronoun in ﴿fi shughul﴾, and ﴿fakihun﴾ [is the predicate], meaning that their wives share with them in that occupation and in that enjoyment, and in reclining upon the couches under the shades.

It was read: ﴿fi zilal﴾ (in shades). The ﴿arika﴾ is the couch within the bridal chamber. [Footnote: "the bridal chamber is the bride's room, decorated with garments and curtains, as in al-Sihah." (ʿAyn)] It was said: it is the bedding within it.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿muttaki'in﴾. ﴿Yadda'una﴾ is of the form yaftaʿilun, from the du'a' (calling/asking), meaning: they ask for it for themselves, like your saying: ishtawa and ijtamala, when he roasted and took for himself. [Footnote: "'ijtamala' — in al-Sihah: I melted the fat, ajmaluhu jamlan, and ijtamaltuhu, meaning I melted it." (ʿAyn)] Labid said:

"Then he roasted [meat] on a windy night and took for himself"

[Translation of the poem as given in the commentary:]
"And a youth whom his mother sent to us with a message, so we gave him what he asked.
She sent him, and his provision came to him; so he roasted on a windy night and took for himself."

These are by Labid ibn Rabi'a. [Footnote: "al-alūk" means the message; i.e., "how many a youth whom his mother sent to us with a message," which here means the request. We gave him what he asked for the food immediately upon his asking, and he explained that by saying: "She sent him, and his provision came to him," and this indicates that they had no food when the youth came to them; i.e., his provision came to him from the hunt, so he roasted meat for himself on a dark windy night in which generosity is scarce, and took much of it for himself and for his mother who had sent him. It is also narrated as "ijtamala" with a jim, and in al-Sihah: "jamaltu al-shahm wa-ijtamaltuhu" when I melted it; and this narration is more fitting and more useful.]

It may also mean "yatadā'ūnahu" (they call for it to one another), as in your saying: "irtamāhu" and "tarāmāhu" (they threw it to one another). It was said: it means "yatamannawn" (they wish for), from the saying: "idda' ʿalayya mā shi'ta" (ask of me whatever you wish), meaning "tamannahu ʿalayya" (wish it of me), and "fulān fī khayr mā iddaʿā" (so-and-so is in the best of what he wished), that is, in the best of what he desired. Al-Zajjaj said: it is from the du'a', meaning: what the people of the Garden call for will come to them.

﴿Salam﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿mā yaddaʿūn﴾, as if He said to them: "Peace will be said to them," ﴿a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. The meaning is that Allah greets them with peace through the angels, or without an intermediary, as a magnification of their honour; and that is what they wish for, and they will have it, and none will withhold it from them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the angels enter upon them with the greeting from the Lord of the worlds. It was said: ﴿mā yaddaʿūn﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿salam﴾ is its predicate, meaning: for them is what they call for, pure and unmixed, without any defect in it. And ﴿qawlan﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) of emphasis (ta'kid) for the divine saying ﴿wa-lahum ma yaddaʿūn﴾, [and] ﴿salam﴾, meaning: a promise from a Lord, Most Merciful. The most appropriate view is that it is in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas, a grammatical specification of an unnamed term), and that is one of its figures of speech. It was read ﴿salm﴾, which has the meaning of ﴿salam﴾ in both senses. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿salaman﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: for them is what they desire, sincerely.
