Wa-imtāzū (and separate yourselves) and withdraw from the believers, and stand apart; and that is when the believers are gathered and conducted to Paradise. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, that day they will be divided. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful; and as for those who disbelieved…﴾ [30:14–16], to the end of the verse. It is said: māzahu, fa-nmāza, wa-imtāza (he separated it, so it separated, and it became distinct).

And from Qatādah: they withdrew from every good. And from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: for each disbeliever there is a house of Fire in which he dwells; he neither sees nor is seen. Its meaning: some of them become separated from others.

The covenant (al-'ahd): the charge or command. "'Ahida ilayhi" means he charged him, when he commanded him. The covenant of God with them (ʿahd Allah ilayhim) is what He established in them of the proofs of reason (adillat al-'aql) and what He sent down to them of the indications of revelation (dala'il al-sam'). Worshipping Satan ('ibadat al-shaytan) means obeying him in what he whispers to them and makes attractive to them.

It has been read as i'had, with the hamza vowelled with a kasra. Every verb of the pattern fa'ala (bab fa'ala) permits a kasra in the letters of its imperfect prefix, except the yaʾ. [[His words "fi huruf mudari'ihi al-kasr" are perhaps "mudari'ihi" (the imperfect). (ʿ)]]

It has also been read as a'had, with the ha vowelled with a kasra. Al-Zajjaj permitted that it be of the pattern na'ima yan'amu and darraba yadribu. It has been read as ahhad, with a ha. And it has been read as ahad, which is the dialect of Tamim. From it comes their saying "daha, maha" [[His words "and from it their saying daha maha": i.e., leave it with it. (ʿ)]].

This (hadha) refers to what was charged to them: disobeying Satan and obeying the Most Merciful, since there is no straighter path than it. The indefiniteness (al-tankir) in it is like what is in the verse of Kuthayyir:

If she who gives the coolness of her upper teeth, the lofty ones, ...
then I am poorer than I am, for indeed I am poor.

How many are the reports that she has married,
so will a bearer of good news come to me with divorce?

It is said to be for Kuthayyir, for the sake of ʿAzza. It is also said to be for Majnun Layla. His words "I did not call in ignorance" (ma jahiltuha) mean that it was from deliberate intent and an attentive heart. His words "li-in kana yahdi" are an explanation of the call (al-da'wa), and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) for emphasis and to convey that the call was made in secret. That is, "if she gives the coolness of her upper teeth." He singled them out because they are the ones that show most often. It is also said that al-ʿula means "the noble." "Li-ahwaju minni" means: indeed I am extremely poor, so I have more right to it than any needy person, because I am the neediest of people to it. It is permissible that "anyabaha" (her fangs) be a metonym for her whole self. "Wa-innani la-faqir" is a statement used in the sense of an imperative (inshaʾ) by way of metaphor (majaz mursal), because showing extreme need implies a request. It is also permissible that it be a metonym for it, and that it is the answer to an oath indicated by the lam. The answer to the condition is omitted, obligatorily, because what is mentioned indicates it. "Ma" is exclamatory (ta'ajjubiyya), "akthar" is an exclamatory verb, "al-akhbar" is its object, "an" is the lightened form of the heavy one, its noun is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and it is in the position of a preposition. That is: I marvel at the great number of reports informing of her marriage. "Hal" is an interrogative used in the sense of wishing (tamanni) or, by metaphor (majaz mursal) through the relation of general request, in the sense of marvelling: I wish for that, or I marvel at its absence.

He meant: "indeed I am poor," poor to an extreme degree, deserving to be described by it because its conditions are complete in me; otherwise the meaning of the verse would not be sound. Likewise His words ﴿ This is a straight path ﴾ mean: a path that is perfect in its kind, perfect in its straightness, comprising every condition it must have. It is also permissible that it be meant: "This is a part of the straight paths," as a rebuke to them for deviating from it and avoiding its way, just as people avoid a crooked road that leads to misguidance and destruction. As if it were said: the least state of the road that is the straightest of roads is that one should believe in it as one believes in the road which does not lead the traveller astray. As a man says to his son, when he has given him the most complete advice, beyond which there is none: "This, in my opinion, is the word of a beneficial adviser who is not harmful," rebuking him for turning away from his counsel.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 36, verses 62–64:

It is recited as "jibillan" (jibillan), with two dammas, and with a damma and a sukun, and with two dammas and a shaddah, and with two kasras, and with a kasra and a sukun, and with two kasras and a shaddah. These forms all have the meaning of "creation" (khalq). It is also recited as "jibalan," the plural of "jibla" (jibla), like "fitar" and "khalq."

In the recitation attributed to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "jilan wahidan" (jilan wahidan), a single generation, not "ajyal" (ajyal, plural of jil, generations).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verse 67:

Al-tams (ṭams): obliterating the cleft of the eye so that it becomes smooth, effaced.

﴿فَاسْتَبَقُوا الصِّرَاطَ﴾ cannot be other than one of the following: it is either with the preposition elided and the verb made to reach its object, the original being "fa-istabaqū ilā al-ṣirāṭ" (so they raced toward the path); or the verb is taken to imply the meaning of "ibtadarū" (they hastened to).

Or the ṣirāṭ is made the thing raced from, not the thing raced to; or it is put in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf). The meaning is: if He had willed, He would have obliterated their eyes, so that if they tried to race toward the clear road (al-ṭarīq al-mahya‘) [[His words "ilā al-ṭarīq al-mahya‘": al-hay‘ah in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-hiyū‘ is cowardice, and al-hay‘ah is melting, flowing, and everything that frightens you of a sound, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. Perhaps what is meant is the one made easy by its frequent use. (ʿA.)]] which they were accustomed to traveling, to their dwellings and to their familiar destinations to which they returned often—just as they used to race toward it, hastening (mūḍi‘īn) [[His words "mūḍi‘īn": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: waḍaʿa al-baʿīr and other than it: he hastened from its pace, and awḍaʿahu rākibuhu (its rider made it hasten). (ʿA.)]] in their affairs of worldly life—they would not be able, and it would be beyond them to see and to know the direction of the way, let alone anything else.

Or: if He had willed, He would have blinded them, so that if they wished to walk racing along the familiar path—as was their constant habit—they would not be able to. Or: if He had willed, He would have blinded them, so that if they sought to pass beyond the path they were accustomed to walking on, they would be unable and would not know a way. That is, they are only able to travel the customary road, not what lies beyond it of the other roads and routes, just as you see the blind guided in what they are familiar with and have become used to [[His words "wa-ḍarrū bihi": i.e., they became accustomed to it. (ʿA.)]] of destinations, and not in others.

﴿عَلَى مَكَانَتِهِمْ﴾ — it is also read as "ʿalā makānātihim" (on their places). Al-makānah and al-makān are one and the same, like al-maqāmah and al-maqām. That is:

We would have transformed them into a transformation that freezes them in their place, so that they cannot go away from it, neither advancing nor retreating, neither going forward nor returning.

There is disagreement about the transformation (al-maskh). From Ibn ʿAbbās: "We would have transformed them into apes and swine." It was also said: into stones. From Qatādah: "We would have made them sit upon their feet and rendered them disabled."

It is also read as "muḍiyyan" with the three vowel-harakat, so al-maḍiyy and al-maḍī are like al-ʿatiyy and al-ʿatī, and al-maḍiyy is like al-ṣabiyy.

Nunakkishu fi al-khalq: We reverse him in creation, i.e., We turn him around in it, so that We create him in the opposite of the way We created him before. That is because We created him in weakness of body and emptiness of intellect and knowledge, then We made him grow, passing from state to state and rising from degree to degree, until he reaches his full strength (ashudd) and completes his power, and understands and knows what is for him and what is against him. Then, when he reaches that point, We reverse him in creation and make him diminish, until he returns to a state resembling that of a child in weakness of body, lack of understanding, and emptiness of knowledge, just as an arrow is reversed so that its top becomes its bottom.

The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation; will they not then understand?﴾ and ﴿And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that after knowledge he knows nothing.﴾ [Qur'an 16:70; 22:5] Then ﴿We returned him to the lowest of the low.﴾ [Qur'an 95:5]

This is a proof that the One who moves them from youth to old age, from strength to weakness, from soundness of intellect to senility and poor discernment, and from knowledge to ignorance, after having moved them in the opposite direction and reversal of this movement, is able to obliterate their eyes, transform them in their places, and do with them whatever He wills and intends.

It has been read with a kasra on the kaf (nunakkisahu / nunkisahu, i.e., "we reverse him"), and "nunakkisahu" and "nunkisahu," from al-tankis and al-inkas. (Note: his remark "read with a kasra on the kaf" indicates that the well-known reading is with a damma on the kaf; both come from al-nakas.)

Will they not then understand? Read with the ya' and with the ta'.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 36, verses 69–70:

They used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "He is a poet." It is related that the one who said it was ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt. Then [Allah] said: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾, i.e., We did not teach him poetry by teaching him the Qur'an, meaning: the Qur'an is not poetry and is not of poetry in any way. And how could it be? Poetry is only speech that is metrical and rhymed, that indicates a meaning. So where is the meter? Where is the rhyme? Where are the meanings that poets aim at, compared with its meanings? Where is the arrangement of their speech compared with its arrangement and its styles? So, when investigated, there is no connection between it and poetry, except that its words are Arabic, just as that [poetry] is too. ﴿And it is not befitting for him﴾, i.e., it is not proper for him nor would he be able to do it even if he sought to. That is, We made him such that if he wished to compose poetry it would not come to him or be easy for him, just as We made him unlettered, unable to write or to do it well, so that the proof would be more established and the doubt more refuted. It is related from al-Khalil that: "Poetry was dearer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than much speech, but it did not come to him."

If you say: [what about] his saying:

"I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib." [Agreed upon, from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib in a hadith.]

And his saying: [Agreed upon, from the hadith of Jundub ibn Sufyan in a hadith.]

"Are you anything but a finger that bled, and what you have suffered is in the way of Allah?"

"O soul, do not despair of my death; this is the reservoir of death, you have reached it.
What you wished for has come to you; if you do what they did, you will be guided."

These are verses of ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha when he carried the banner after the killing of Zayd ibn Harithah and Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, and his finger was struck in the battle and bled. Al-Bukhari related from Jundub that he said: "While the Prophet (ﷺ) was walking, a stone struck him, and he stumbled, and his finger bled, and he said: 'Are you anything but a finger that bled, and what you have suffered is in the way of Allah?'" This informs that he (ﷺ) recited the poetry of another, and it is with a kasra on the taʾ to match the rhyme. Al-Kirmani said: the taʾ in the rajaz is kasra, and in the hadith it is sukun. ʿIyad said: some people were heedless and narrated "dammayt" and "laqayt" without the madd, contradicting the narration. Ahmad and al-Tayalisi related that he (ﷺ) said it while he was going out to prayer. "Dammayt" is an adjective of "uṣbaʿ" (finger), and the meaning is: nothing of harm has come to you except that you bled, and that was not in vain but was in the way of Allah and His pleasure alone; that is, the harm you suffered is in the way of Allah, so do not grieve. He treated it as a rational being and addressed it thus, as consolation and strengthening for it, though in reality it is for himself. Then he explicitly addressed the soul, affirming it, with his saying: "If you are not killed in battle, there is no escape for you from death, and this is its reservoir, so do not flee from it, for falling into trial is easier than awaiting it." He likened death to a torrent by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), so he attributed to it reservoirs by imagination (takhyil), and likened it to fire likewise, so he attributed to it the "ṣalā," which is plunging into fire. There is no obstacle to likening a thing to two hidden matters, with an allusion to each by what suits it. It is permissible to use "al-ḥiyāḍ" (reservoirs) as a metaphor for the known explicitly. "What you wished for from war, which leads to martyrdom, you have reached. If you do as Zayd and Jaʿfar did, you have been guided to the path of good."

I say: This is nothing but speech of the kind that he used to utter naturally, without artifice or affectation, except that it happened, without his intending it or paying attention to it, to be metrical, just as in many people's speeches, sermons, letters and conversations there occur metrical things that no one calls poetry, and it does not occur to the speaker or the listener that they are poetry. If you examine any speech for something like this, you will find that instances falling into the meters of the bahr are not rare. Moreover, al-Khalil did not count the mashtur of rajaz as poetry. And when [Allah] denied that the Qur'an was of the genre of poetry, He said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: it is nothing but a reminder from Allah the Exalted, by which mankind and the jinn are admonished, as He said: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾. And it is nothing but a Qur'an, a heavenly Book, read in the prayer niches, recited in acts of worship, and by its recitation and acting upon what is in it one attains the success of both abodes. So how great is the difference between it and poetry, which is among the whisperings of the devils?

﴿That it may warn﴾ — the Qur'an, or the Messenger; and it was read "that you may warn" with the ta'. "Yunshira" (warn) is from "nadhara bihi" when one knows of it. ﴿Him who is alive﴾, i.e., rational and reflective, for the heedless is like the dead. Or: whom it is known of him that he will believe and thus live by faith. ﴿And the word will be fulfilled﴾, and the word of punishment will be due ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, who do not reflect and from whom faith is not expected.

There is no obstacle to likening a thing to two hidden matters, with an allusion to each by what suits it. It is permissible to use "al-ḥiyāḍ" (reservoirs) as a metaphor for the known explicitly. "What you wished for from war, which leads to martyrdom, you have reached. If you do as Zayd and Jaʿfar did, you have been guided to the path of good."

I say: This is nothing but speech of the kind that he used to utter naturally, without artifice or affectation, except that it happened, without his intending it or paying attention to it, to be metrical, just as in many people's speeches, sermons, letters and conversations there occur metrical things that no one calls poetry, and it does not occur to the speaker or the listener that they are poetry. If you examine any speech for something like this, you will find that instances falling into the meters of the bahr are not rare. Moreover, al-Khalil did not count the mashtur of rajaz as poetry. And when [Allah] denied that the Qur'an was of the genre of poetry, He said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: it is nothing but a reminder from Allah the Exalted, by which mankind and the jinn are admonished, as He said: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾. And it is nothing but a Qur'an, a heavenly Book, read in the prayer niches, recited in acts of worship, and by its recitation and acting upon what is in it one attains the success of both abodes. So how great is the difference between it and poetry, which is among the whisperings of the devils?

﴿That it may warn﴾ — the Qur'an, or the Messenger; and it was read "that you may warn" with the ta'. "Yunshira" (warn) is from "nadhara bihi" when one knows of it. ﴿Him who is alive﴾, i.e., rational and reflective, for the heedless is like the dead. Or: whom it is known of him that he will believe and thus live by faith. ﴿And the word will be fulfilled﴾, and the word of punishment will be due ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, who do not reflect and from whom faith is not expected.

فارقنا قبل أن نفارقه ... لما قضى من جماعنا وطرا

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, on Surah Yasin, verses 74–76:

They took the gods out of hope that they would be strengthened by them and supported by their standing. But the matter is the reverse of what they assumed: they are an army made ready for their gods, brought forward (﴿muhḍarūn﴾), serving them, defending them, and angry on their behalf, while the gods have no capacity or power to give victory. Or they took them so that they would help them with God and intercede for them, but the matter is contrary to what they imagined: on the Day of Resurrection they are an army made ready for them, brought forward for their punishment, because they will be made fuel for the Fire.

It has been read ﴿fa-lā yaḥzunka﴾ with the yāʾ vowelled both with a fatḥa and with a ḍamma, from ḥazinahu and aḥzanahu (both meaning "to grieve/sadden"). The meaning is: do not let their denial, their harm, and their harshness concern you, for We know what they conceal from you of their enmity, ﴿and what they reveal﴾, and We will requite them for it. It is therefore fitting for someone like you to find consolation in this warning, and to call to mind in himself the image of his own condition and theirs in the Hereafter, until worry clears away from him and grief does not overtake him.

If you ask: what do you say about one who says that if a reader recites ﴿anā naʿlamu﴾ with a fatḥa (on the hamza of inna), his prayer is invalidated, and if he believes what that reading gives as meaning, he has disbelieved? I answer: there are two aspects to this.

The first: it is on the omission of the lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl, the particle of purpose or reason). This is frequent in the Qur'an, in poetry, and in every speech and in regular analogy. Its meaning and the meaning of the kasra are the same. Upon this is the talbiyah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Indeed the praise and the blessing are Yours," with the kasra according to Abu Hanifa and the fatḥa according to al-Shafiʿi, and both are a causal construction.

The second: that it is in apposition (badal) to ﴿qawluhum﴾ ("their saying"), as if it were said: ﴿fa-lā yaḥzunka, inna naʿlamu mā yusirrūna wa mā yuʿlinūn﴾ ("do not let their saying grieve you; We know what they conceal and what they reveal"). This meaning also holds with the kasra, if you make it the object of the verb of saying.

It is thus clear that the connection of grief with God's being knowing, and its absence, do not depend on the kasra or fatḥa of inna, but depend on your interpretation. So you distinguish: if it is fatḥa, you interpret it as the meaning of causation and do not interpret it as apposition, just as you distinguish when it is kasra by interpreting the meaning of causation and not the meaning of being an object. Then, whether you read it with kasra or fatḥa, the matter that made that speaker consider the issue so grave is nothing more than the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) prohibition from grieving over God's knowledge of their secret and their open conduct, and the prohibition of this does not require anything. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾, and ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾, and ﴿and do not invoke with God another god﴾?

Then, whether you read it with kasra or fatḥa, the matter that made that speaker consider the issue so grave is nothing more than the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) prohibition from grieving over God's knowledge of their secret and their open conduct, and the prohibition of this does not require anything. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾, and ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾, and ﴿and do not invoke with God another god﴾?

Almighty God has condemned their denial of the Resurrection with a condemnation more astonishing and more eloquent than any other, and it is more indicative of the persistence of man's disbelief, his excess in denying blessings and his ingratitude for favours, his immersion in baseness, and his penetration into shamelessness [[On his words "and his penetration into shamelessness": in al-Sihah, "waqaha al-rajul qahatan wa waqahatan" means that the man became lacking in modesty (ع)]]. He established against them that their substance from which He created them is the basest and most contemptible of things: the vile drop of semen that issues from the urethra, which is the channel of impurity. Then He marvelled at their state, that such a one, despite the lowliness of his origin and the meanness of his beginning, should confront the Almighty in disputation, lift up his face [[On his words "lift up his face ..." in al-Sihah, "al-sharz" means harshness, which is roughness; "al-mahk" means obstinacy (ع)] to argue, mount the back of falsehood and persist, and say: "Who can give life to the bones when they have decayed?" This is the obstinacy beyond which there is no aspiration.

It is related that a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, among them Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, Abu Jahl, al-As ibn Wa'il and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, discussed this matter. Ubayy said to them: "Do you not see what Muhammad says, that God resurrects the dead?" Then he said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will go to him and dispute with him," and he took a decayed bone and began crumbling it in his hand, saying:

"O Muhammad, do you think God will give life to this after it has decayed?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and admit you into Hell" [[Al-Halabi mentioned this from Qatadah without a chain. al-Hakim transmitted it from the narration of Abu Bishr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas: "that al-As ibn Wa'il took a bone from al-Batha', crumbled it in his hand, then said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: 'Will God give life to this after it has decayed?' He said: 'Yes, God will cause you to die...' - the hadith." al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related through Husayn from Abu Malik, who said: "Ubayy ibn Khalaf came with a rotten bone - the hadith." Ibn Mardawayh related through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Abu Jahl came with a decayed bone."]]

It is also said that the meaning of His words ﴿Then, behold, he is an open adversary﴾ is: then, behold, he is, after having been a despised drop of water, a discerning man, capable of disputation, eloquent, clearly expressing what is in his soul, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who is brought up among ornaments and is not clear in dispute [...]?﴾

If you ask: why did He call His words ﴿Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?﴾ a parable? I say: because of the amazing story it indicates, which resembles a parable, namely the denial of God's power to revive the dead. Or because of the comparison it contains, since what they deny is of the kind of thing by which God is described as capable, on the evidence of the first creation. So when it is said, "Who will give life to the bones?" in the manner of denial, so that this would be among the things by which God is described as being able, it amounts to rendering God powerless and likening Him to His creatures, in that they are not described as able to do it.

﴿Al-rameem﴾ is a noun for what has decayed of the bones, not an attribute, like al-rummah and al-rufat. So one cannot say: why was it not feminine, when it occurs as the predicate of a feminine noun? Nor is it an fa'il in the sense of fa'il or maf'ul. This verse has been cited by those who affirm that bones have life and say that the bones of a dead animal are impure, because death affects them before life leaves them. The followers of Abu Hanifah, however, hold that they are pure, and likewise the horn and sinew; they claim that life does not inhere in them, so death does not affect them. They say: the meaning of "giving life to the bones" in the verse is returning them to what they were, soft and moist in a living, sensitive body.

﴿And He is the Knower of every creation﴾: He knows how to create. Nothing of the creation of the things brought into being or the things returned, nor of their kinds, types, great and minute, is too much for Him.

Then He mentioned among the wonders of His creation the kindling of fire from the green tree, despite fire's opposition to water and its extinction by it. These are the flint sticks with which property is set alight, most of them being of al-Markh and al-Affar. In their proverbs: "In every tree there is fire." They praise al-Markh and al-Affar: a man cuts two green branches of them like tooth-sticks, both still moist, dripping water; he rubs al-Markh, which is male, against al-Affar, which is female, and fire is kindled by God's permission.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "There is no tree except that fire is in it, except the jujube." [[I have not found it.]] They said:

That is why it is used for the fuller's washing-stones. It was read ﴿al-akhdar﴾ (the green), following the wording, and read ﴿al-khadra'﴾ (the green, feminine), following the meaning. A similar usage is His words: ﴿from a tree of zaqqum, of which you will eat and fill your bellies, and then drink upon it of boiling water﴾. Whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth despite their great magnitude is even more able to create human beings. Its meaning is also His words: ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾. It was read ﴿yaqdir﴾ (is able). His words ﴿that He should create their likes﴾ admit of two meanings: that He should create their likes in smallness and insignificance in comparison with the heavens and the earth, or that He should restore them, since the return is like the beginning though not identical with it. ﴿And He is the Creator, the Knower﴾, the one of many creatures, the one of many things known. It was read ﴿al-Khaliq﴾ (the Creator).

﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾: when a call of wisdom summons Him to bring it into existence, with no obstacle, He says to it "Be" that it may be, without delay, ﴿and it is﴾, that is, it comes into being, existing without doubt. If you ask: what is the reality of His words, "He says to it, 'Be,' and it is"? I say: it is a figure of speech and an image, because nothing among created things is beyond Him, and He is like the obedient subordinate when the command of an obeyed commander reaches him. If you ask: what is the reasoning behind the two readings of "fa-yakun" (and it is)? I say: as for the nominative, it is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, its estimated form being "fa-huwa yakun" (so He is making it be), coordinated with a similar clause, namely His command that He say to it "Be." As for the accusative, it is coordinated with "yaqul" (He says). The meaning is: nothing that applies to bodies is permissible for Him, when they act upon something they are able to do, through touching the locus of power, using instruments, and what follows from that of hardship, fatigue and weariness. His command, rather, is to one who is Almighty and Knowing by His very essence, that He make His summons to action effective, so that it comes into being. How, then, could One like this be incapable of something feasible, so as to be incapable of resurrection?

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: a declaration of His transcendence above what the polytheists ascribe to Him, and an expression of wonder that they should say about Him what they say. ﴿In whose hand is the dominion of everything﴾: He is the owner of everything and the one who disposes of it according to the requirements of His will and the decrees of His wisdom. It was read ﴿malakut﴾ and ﴿malakah﴾ and ﴿malik﴾, and the meaning is one. ﴿You will be returned﴾ was read with the "t" both vowelled with a damma and with a fatha.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "I did not know what was narrated about the virtues of Ya-Sin and its recitation, how it was singled out, until I found it in this verse."

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every thing has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin seeking the Face of God, God will forgive him, and he will be given a reward as if he had recited the Qur'an twenty-two times. Any Muslim before whom Ya-Sin is recited when the Angel of Death comes down to him, there descend upon him for each letter of it ten angels who stand before him in rows, pray for him, ask forgiveness for him, witness his washing, follow his bier, pray over him and witness his burial. Any Muslim who recites Ya-Sin while in the agonies of death, the Angel of Death does not take his soul until Ridwan, the keeper of Paradise, gives him life with a drink of the drinks of Paradise, which he drinks while on his bed; then the Angel of Death takes his soul while he is sated, and he remains in his grave sated, and he does not need any of the pools of the Prophets until he enters Paradise, sated." [[Transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tha'labi from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Its beginning is in al-Tirmidhi through Harun Abu Muhammad from Muqatil ibn Hayyan from Qatadah from Anas, and he said: "Gharib." Harun is unknown. There are also traditions on this from Abu Bakr and Abu Hurayrah. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is transmitted by al-Bazzar, in which Humayd al-Makki, client of the family of 'Alqamah, appears, and he is weak. The hadith of Abu Bakr is transmitted by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi.]]

He, upon whom be blessings and peace, also said: "Indeed, in the Qur'an there is a sura whose reciter will intercede and whose hearer will be forgiven. Truly, it is the sura of Ya-Sin." [[Transmitted by al-Tha'labi through Muhammad ibn 'Umayr from Hisham from his father from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her.]]

He said: 'Yes, God will cause you to die...' - the hadith." al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related through Husayn from Abu Malik, who said: "Ubayy ibn Khalaf came with a rotten bone - the hadith." If you ask: why did He call His words ﴿Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?﴾ a parable? I say: because of the amazing story it indicates, which resembles a parable, namely the denial of God's power to revive the dead. Or because of the comparison it contains, since what they deny is of the kind of thing by which God is described as capable, on the evidence of the first creation. So when it is said, "Who will give life to the bones?" in the manner of denial, so that this would be among the things by which God is described as being able, it amounts to rendering God powerless and likening Him to His creatures, in that they are not described as able to do it.

﴿Al-rameem﴾ is a noun for what has decayed of the bones, not an attribute, like al-rummah and al-rufat. So one cannot say: why was it not feminine, when it occurs as the predicate of a feminine noun? Nor is it an fa'il in the sense of fa'il or maf'ul. This verse has been cited by those who affirm that bones have life and say that the bones of a dead animal are impure, because death affects them before life leaves them. The followers of Abu Hanifah, however, hold that they are pure, and likewise the horn and sinew; they claim that life does not inhere in them, so death does not affect them. They say: the meaning of "giving life to the bones" in the verse is returning them to what they were, soft and moist in a living, sensitive body.

They praise al-Markh and al-Affar: a man cuts two green branches of them like tooth-sticks, both still moist, dripping water; he rubs al-Markh, which is male, against al-Affar, which is female, and fire is kindled by God's permission.

That is why it is used for the fuller's washing-stones. It was read ﴿al-akhdar﴾ (the green), following the wording, and read ﴿al-khadra'﴾ (the green, feminine), following the meaning. Whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth despite their great magnitude is even more able to create human beings. Its meaning is also His words: ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾. It was read ﴿yaqdir﴾ (is able). ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾: when a call of wisdom summons Him to bring it into existence, with no obstacle, He says to it "Be" that it may be, without delay, ﴿and it is﴾, that is, it comes into being, existing without doubt. If you ask: what is the reality of His words, "He says to it, 'Be,' and it is"? I say: it is a figure of speech and an image, because nothing among created things is beyond Him, and He is like the obedient subordinate when the command of an obeyed commander reaches him. If you ask: what is the reasoning behind the two readings of "fa-yakun" (and it is)? I say: as for the nominative, it is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, its estimated form being "fa-huwa yakun" (so He is making it be), coordinated with a similar clause, namely His command that He say to it "Be." As for the accusative, it is coordinated with "yaqul" (He says). The meaning is: nothing that applies to bodies is permissible for Him, when they act upon something they are able to do, through touching the locus of power, using instruments, and what follows from that of hardship, fatigue and weariness. His command, rather, is to one who is Almighty and Knowing by His very essence, that He make His summons to action effective, so that it comes into being. How, then, could One like this be incapable of something feasible, so as to be incapable of resurrection?

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: a declaration of His transcendence above what the polytheists ascribe to Him, and an expression of wonder that they should say about Him what they say. ﴿In whose hand is the dominion of everything﴾: He is the owner of everything and the one who disposes of it according to the requirements of His will and the decrees of His wisdom. It was read ﴿malakut﴾ and ﴿malakah﴾ and ﴿malik﴾, and the meaning is one. ﴿You will be returned﴾ was read with the "t" both vowelled with a damma and with a fatha.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "I did not know what was narrated about the virtues of Ya-Sin and its recitation, how it was singled out, until I found it in this verse."

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every thing has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin seeking the Face of God, God will forgive him, and he will be given a reward as if he had recited the Qur'an twenty-two times. Any Muslim before whom Ya-Sin is recited when the Angel of Death comes down to him, there descend upon him for each letter of it ten angels who stand before him in rows, pray for him, ask forgiveness for him, witness his washing, follow his bier, pray over him and witness his burial. Any Muslim who recites Ya-Sin while in the agonies of death, the Angel of Death does not take his soul until Ridwan, the keeper of Paradise, gives him life with a drink of the drinks of Paradise, which he drinks while on his bed; then the Angel of Death takes his soul while he is sated, and he remains in his grave sated, and he does not need any of the pools of the Prophets until he enters Paradise, sated." [[Transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tha'labi from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Its beginning is in al-Tirmidhi through Harun Abu Muhammad from Muqatil ibn Hayyan from Qatadah from Anas, and he said: "Gharib." Harun is unknown. There are also traditions on this from Abu Bakr and Abu Hurayrah. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is transmitted by al-Bazzar, in which Humayd al-Makki, client of the family of 'Alqamah, appears, and he is weak. The hadith of Abu Bakr is transmitted by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi.]]

He, upon whom be blessings and peace, also said: "Indeed, in the Qur'an there is a sura whose reciter will intercede and whose hearer will be forgiven. Truly, it is the sura of Ya-Sin." [[Transmitted by al-Tha'labi through Muhammad ibn 'Umayr from Hisham from his father from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her.]]

Almighty God has condemned their denial of the Resurrection with a condemnation more astonishing and more eloquent than any other, and it is more indicative of the persistence of man's disbelief, his excess in denying blessings and his ingratitude for favours, his immersion in baseness, and his penetration into shamelessness [[On his words "and his penetration into shamelessness": in al-Sihah, "waqaha al-rajul qahatan wa waqahatan" means that the man became lacking in modesty (ع)]]. He established against them that their substance from which He created them is the basest and most contemptible of things: the vile drop of semen that issues from the urethra, which is the channel of impurity. Then He marvelled at their state, that such a one, despite the lowliness of his origin and the meanness of his beginning, should confront the Almighty in disputation, lift up his face [[On his words "lift up his face ..." in al-Sihah, "al-sharz" means harshness, which is roughness; "al-mahk" means obstinacy (ع)] to argue, mount the back of falsehood and persist, and say: "Who can give life to the bones when they have decayed?" Then his dispute concerns the most binding attribute of him and the most closely attached to him, which is that he was originated from lifelessness, while he denies his own origination from lifelessness. This is the obstinacy beyond which there is no aspiration.

It is related that a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, among them Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, Abu Jahl, al-As ibn Wa'il and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, discussed this matter. Ubayy said to them: "Do you not see what Muhammad says, that God resurrects the dead?" Then he said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will go to him and dispute with him," and he took a decayed bone and began crumbling it in his hand, saying:

"O Muhammad, do you think God will give life to this after it has decayed?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and admit you into Hell" [[Al-Halabi mentioned this from Qatadah without a chain. al-Hakim transmitted it from the narration of Abu Bishr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas: "that al-As ibn Wa'il took a bone from al-Batha', crumbled it in his hand, then said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: 'Will God give life to this after it has decayed?' He said: 'Yes, God will cause you to die...' - the hadith." al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related through Husayn from Abu Malik, who said: "Ubayy ibn Khalaf came with a rotten bone - the hadith." Ibn Mardawayh related through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Abu Jahl came with a decayed bone."]]

It is also said that the meaning of His words ﴿Then, behold, he is an open adversary﴾ is: then, behold, he is, after having been a despised drop of water, a discerning man, capable of disputation, eloquent, clearly expressing what is in his soul, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who is brought up among ornaments and is not clear in dispute [...]?﴾

If you ask: why did He call His words ﴿Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?﴾ a parable? I say: because of the amazing story it indicates, which resembles a parable, namely the denial of God's power to revive the dead. Or because of the comparison it contains, since what they deny is of the kind of thing by which God is described as capable, on the evidence of the first creation. So when it is said, "Who will give life to the bones?" in the manner of denial, so that this would be among the things by which God is described as being able, it amounts to rendering God powerless and likening Him to His creatures, in that they are not described as able to do it.

﴿Al-rameem﴾ is a noun for what has decayed of the bones, not an attribute, like al-rummah and al-rufat. So one cannot say: why was it not feminine, when it occurs as the predicate of a feminine noun? Nor is it an fa'il in the sense of fa'il or maf'ul. This verse has been cited by those who affirm that bones have life and say that the bones of a dead animal are impure, because death affects them before life leaves them. The followers of Abu Hanifah, however, hold that they are pure, and likewise the horn and sinew; they claim that life does not inhere in them, so death does not affect them. They say: the meaning of "giving life to the bones" in the verse is returning them to what they were, soft and moist in a living, sensitive body.

﴿And He is the Knower of every creation﴾: He knows how to create. Nothing of the creation of the things brought into being or the things returned, nor of their kinds, types, great and minute, is too much for Him.

Then He mentioned among the wonders of His creation the kindling of fire from the green tree, despite fire's opposition to water and its extinction by it. These are the flint sticks with which property is set alight, most of them being of al-Markh and al-Affar. In their proverbs: "In every tree there is fire." They praise al-Markh and al-Affar: a man cuts two green branches of them like tooth-sticks, both still moist, dripping water; he rubs al-Markh, which is male, against al-Affar, which is female, and fire is kindled by God's permission.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "There is no tree except that fire is in it, except the jujube." [[I have not found it.]] They said:

That is why it is used for the fuller's washing-stones. It was read ﴿al-akhdar﴾ (the green), following the wording, and read ﴿al-khadra'﴾ (the green, feminine), following the meaning. A similar usage is His words: ﴿from a tree of zaqqum, of which you will eat and fill your bellies, and then drink upon it of boiling water﴾. Whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth despite their great magnitude is even more able to create human beings.
